subject: English
title: Arun and Maya's Big and Small Letter Quest
hook: Arun and Maya discover when to use big (capital) and small letters!

slides.title: Big Letters are Called CAPITALS
slides.storyContext: At school, the teacher shows Arun and Maya a big 'A' and a small 'a' on the board.

points.label: Capital Letter
points.text: The BIG letter form is called a CAPITAL letter

slides.inSimpleWords: Big letters are called CAPITAL letters!

image.alt: Big Letters are Called CAPITALS — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Every Sentence Starts with Capital
slides.storyContext: Maya reads: 'My name is Maya.' Arun points to the big 'M' at the start!

points.label: Rule 1
points.text: Every sentence ALWAYS starts with a capital letter

slides.inSimpleWords: Start sentences with a BIG capital letter!

image.alt: Every Sentence Starts with Capital — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Names Get Capital Letters
slides.storyContext: Arun writes his name: ARUN. Maya writes hers: MAYA. They use capitals!

points.label: Rule 2
points.text: Names of people ALWAYS start with a capital letter

slides.inSimpleWords: Names start with capital letters always!

image.alt: Names Get Capital Letters — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Places Need Capitals Too
slides.storyContext: Maya says 'I live in Delhi.' Arun says 'I live in Mumbai.' Both cities start with capitals!

points.label: Rule 3
points.text: Names of places ALWAYS start with a capital letter

slides.inSimpleWords: City and country names start with capitals!

image.alt: Places Need Capitals Too — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Days and Months Need Capitals
slides.storyContext: Arun says 'Monday is the first day.' Maya says 'January is the first month.' Both use capitals!

points.label: Rule 4
points.text: Days and months ALWAYS start with a capital letter

slides.inSimpleWords: Days and months start with big capital letters!

image.alt: Days and Months Need Capitals — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Capital or Small Letter?
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya play a game: when do we use capitals?

example.problem: Write: i like eating apples on monday
example.solution: I like eating apples on Monday. (Start + name 'I' + day 'Monday' need capitals)

slides.inSimpleWords: Capital at start, names, places, days, months!

image.alt: Capital or Small Letter? — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Small Letters for Most Words
slides.storyContext: Maya explains: most words use small letters in the middle of a sentence!

points.label: Rule 5
points.text: Words in the middle of sentences use SMALL letters

slides.inSimpleWords: Use small letters for most words in a sentence!

image.alt: Small Letters for Most Words — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: Capital and Small Letters
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya write their 'Capital Letter Rules' poster!

points.label: Use CAPITALS for
points.text: Start of sentence, names, places, days, months

points.label: Use SMALL for
points.text: Most other words in the middle

slides.inSimpleWords: Capitals at start, names, places. Smalls for others!

image.alt: Capital and Small Letters — Capital and Small Letters

slides.title: What is a Capital Letter?
slides.storyContext: Let's understand what makes a letter 'capital' or 'small.'

points.label: Capital (uppercase)
points.text: Large, bigger size: A B C D E F G H I J K

points.label: Small (lowercase)
points.text: Small, regular size: a b c d e f g h i j k

slides.inSimpleWords: Capital letters are BIGGER. Small letters are regular size.

slides.title: The Special 'I'
slides.storyContext: The word 'I' (meaning yourself) is always a capital letter, even in the middle!

points.label: Always capital
points.text: I am happy. You and I like to play.

points.label: Remember
points.text: 'I' stands alone as a capital letter, never lowercase

slides.inSimpleWords: The word 'I' is ALWAYS a capital letter!

slides.title: Fix the Capitals - Exercise 1
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya fix sentences with wrong capitals.

example.problem: arun and maya live in delhi
example.solution: Arun and Maya live in Delhi. (Names and cities start with capitals)

slides.inSimpleWords: Always check: start, names, places, days need capitals!

slides.title: Fix the Capitals - Exercise 2
slides.storyContext: Maya's turn: more sentences to fix!

example.problem: i go to school on monday
example.solution: I go to school on Monday. (Both 'I' and 'Monday' need capitals)

slides.inSimpleWords: Remember 'I' and day names always get capitals!

slides.title: Write Your Own Sentence
slides.storyContext: Arun challenges Maya: write a sentence using at least one capital letter rule!

points.label: Your turn
points.text: Write about yourself (use 'I'), a friend (capitalize name), and a day (capitalize day)

slides.inSimpleWords: Write a sentence: I + name + day (all with capitals!)

slides.title: Titles Always Start with Capital
slides.storyContext: Maya reads a book titled 'The Adventures of Little Prince.' Every main word starts with capital!

points.label: Book and movie titles
points.text: Important words in titles start with capitals

slides.inSimpleWords: Book titles and movie names use capitals for big words!

slides.title: Practice with Real Sentences
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya check real examples from their textbooks.

example.solution: The cat sat on Saturday. (Start word and day name need capitals)

slides.inSimpleWords: Check every sentence: first word and special words!

slides.title: When NOT to Use Capitals
slides.storyContext: Understanding what doesn't need capitals helps avoid mistakes!

points.label: No capitals for
points.text: Regular action words (run, jump, play) in the middle

points.label: No capitals for
points.text: Colors, animals, foods (unless at start): red, dog, apple

slides.inSimpleWords: Don't use capitals for regular action words!

slides.title: Spot the Mistake
slides.storyContext: Maya finds sentences with wrong capital letters. Can you fix them?

points.label: Wrong
points.text: I like Playing Football On Tuesday

points.label: Right
points.text: I like playing football on Tuesday

slides.inSimpleWords: Only START and special words get capitals!

slides.title: Countries and Cities
slides.storyContext: Arun says 'I live in India.' Maya says 'I live in Bangalore.' All place names start with capitals!

points.label: Countries
points.text: India, France, Japan, Brazil (always capital)

points.label: Cities
points.text: Mumbai, Delhi, Chennai, Pune (always capital)

slides.inSimpleWords: All country and city names start with capitals!

slides.title: Months Matter
slides.storyContext: Arun writes: 'I was born in March.' Let's see all the months!

example.solution: January, February, March, April (all month names start with capitals)

slides.inSimpleWords: Every month name starts with a capital letter!

slides.title: Days of the Week
slides.storyContext: Maya lists all seven days. Every one starts with a capital!

points.label: The seven days
points.text: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday

points.label: Always capital
points.text: Every day of the week needs a big letter

slides.inSimpleWords: All day names start with capital letters!

slides.title: Fill the Blank
slides.storyContext: Can you complete these sentences with capital letters where needed?

points.label: Question 1
points.text: My friend _____ was born on _____. (name + day)

points.label: Question 2
points.text: _____ is a country in Asia. (country name)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use capitals for names, days, and countries!

slides.title: Exclamation and Questions
slides.storyContext: Arun exclaims 'Wow!' Maya asks 'Really?' Both start with capitals even with special marks!

points.label: After ! or ?
points.text: If next sentence starts, use capital letter

slides.inSimpleWords: Even after ! or ? the next sentence starts with a capital!

slides.title: Dialogue Practice
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya have a conversation. Each sentence starts with capital!

example.solution: Arun said 'Hello!' Maya replied 'Hi there!' (names and dialogue start with capitals)

slides.inSimpleWords: In conversations, every sentence and name has capitals!

slides.title: The Grammar Rule Summary
slides.storyContext: A complete list of when capitals are used.

points.label: Always use capitals
points.text: Start of sentence, names, places, days, months, 'I'

points.label: Most other words
points.text: Use small (lowercase) letters in the middle

slides.inSimpleWords: Capitals: first word, names, places, days, months, and 'I'!

slides.title: Create Your Masterpiece Sentence
slides.storyContext: Now you write a perfect sentence with every capital rule!

points.label: Must include
points.text: A name, a day or month, and proper sentence start

slides.inSimpleWords: Write one sentence showing 3 capital letter rules!

slides.title: Arun and Maya's Big Lesson
slides.storyContext: Our friends celebrate learning all about capitals and small letters!

points.label: For every sentence
points.text: Start with a capital, use small letters mostly

points.label: For special words
points.text: Names, places, days, months, 'I' — all need capitals

points.label: Practice rule
points.text: Read your sentences aloud and check every capital!

slides.inSimpleWords: You now know when to use BIG and small letters!

subject: English
title: Arun and Maya's Punctuation Adventure
hook: Learn the magic dots and marks that help sentences tell their story!

slides.title: The Period Stops the Sentence
slides.storyContext: Arun writes 'I like rice' and puts a dot. The sentence stops here!

points.label: Period (.)
points.text: A period stops a sentence. It means the idea is complete

slides.inSimpleWords: A period (.) ends a sentence with a complete idea!

image.alt: The Period Stops the Sentence — Punctuation

slides.title: Question Marks Ask Questions
slides.storyContext: Maya asks 'Do you like tea?' and puts a curvy mark with a dot.

points.label: Question Mark (?)
points.text: A question mark ends a sentence that ASKS something

slides.inSimpleWords: Question mark (?) ends a sentence that asks!

image.alt: Question Marks Ask Questions — Punctuation

slides.title: Exclamation Marks Show Feeling
slides.storyContext: Arun shouts 'What a big snake!' and uses a mark that shows his surprise!

points.label: Exclamation Mark (!)
points.text: An exclamation mark shows excitement or surprise

slides.inSimpleWords: Exclamation mark (!) shows big feelings and excitement!

image.alt: Exclamation Marks Show Feeling — Punctuation

slides.title: Three Sentence Ending Marks
slides.storyContext: Maya draws all three marks and explains when to use each one.

points.label: Period (.)
points.text: Normal sentence

points.label: Question (?)
points.text: Asking sentence

points.label: Exclamation (!)
points.text: Excited sentence

slides.inSimpleWords: Period stops. Question asks. Exclamation shows feeling!

image.alt: Three Sentence Ending Marks — Punctuation

slides.title: Comma Separates Ideas
slides.storyContext: Arun writes 'I like apples, mangoes, and bananas.' The commas help us pause!

points.label: Comma (,)
points.text: A comma separates words or ideas in a list

slides.inSimpleWords: Commas (,) separate items in a list!

image.alt: Comma Separates Ideas — Punctuation

slides.title: Using Punctuation Correctly
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya practice putting the right marks in the right places.

example.problem: I like rice bread and milk
example.solution: I like rice, bread, and milk. (commas separate the list)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use correct punctuation to make sentences clear!

image.alt: Using Punctuation Correctly — Punctuation

slides.title: More Punctuation Marks
slides.storyContext: Maya shows apostrophes (for 'can't') and quotation marks (for what people say)!

points.label: Apostrophe (')
points.text: Apostrophe shows missing letters: can't, don't

points.label: Quotation Marks ('')
points.text: Quotation marks show exactly what someone said

slides.inSimpleWords: Apostrophes and quotes help write correct sentences!

image.alt: More Punctuation Marks — Punctuation

slides.title: Punctuation Marks Matter
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya create a 'Punctuation Helper' chart for their classroom!

points.label: Separators
points.text: , (comma)

points.label: Special marks
points.text: ' (apostrophe), '' (quotes)

slides.inSimpleWords: Every punctuation mark has an important job!

image.alt: Punctuation Marks Matter — Punctuation

slides.title: Understanding Periods
slides.storyContext: A period is more than just a dot—it's a signal that an idea ends.

points.label: Period signals
points.text: A complete thought or idea has finished

points.label: Examples
points.text: I like tea. She plays cricket. The dog is brown.

slides.inSimpleWords: A period (.) marks the end of a complete sentence!

slides.title: Understanding Question Marks
slides.storyContext: Question marks come at the end of sentences that ask for information.

points.label: Question mark signals
points.text: Someone is asking for an answer

points.label: Examples
points.text: Do you like apples? What is your name? How are you?

slides.inSimpleWords: A question mark (?) asks for information!

slides.title: Periods vs. Questions - Practice 1
slides.storyContext: Arun checks which mark to use at the end.

example.problem: I like to play cricket_ Do you play_
example.solution: I like to play cricket. Do you play? (Period for statement, question mark for question)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use . for statements, ? for questions!

slides.title: Exclamation Marks for Excitement
slides.storyContext: Maya writes about something surprising and uses exclamation marks!

example.problem: I won the race_ That was amazing_
example.solution: I won the race! That was amazing! (Exclamation marks show excitement)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use ! for excited or surprising sentences!

slides.title: Commas in Lists
slides.storyContext: When writing a list of items, commas separate each thing clearly.

points.label: List rule
points.text: Put a comma between each item except before the last one

points.label: Example
points.text: pen, pencil, ruler, and eraser

slides.inSimpleWords: Commas separate items in a list!

slides.title: Practice Lists with Commas
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya practice writing lists with correct comma placement.

example.problem: I have a dog a cat and a parrot
example.solution: I have a dog, a cat, and a parrot. (Commas separate the animals)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use commas to separate items in a list!

slides.title: Add the Right Punctuation Mark
slides.storyContext: Can you choose the correct ending mark for each sentence?

points.label: Sentence 1
points.text: Arun is playing football

points.label: Sentence 2
points.text: Do you want to join him

points.label: Sentence 3
points.text: What a wonderful day

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose . ? or ! for each sentence!

slides.title: Apostrophes Make Contractions
slides.storyContext: Maya explains: 'can't' is short for 'cannot' — the apostrophe shows missing letters!

points.label: Contraction
points.text: An apostrophe replaces missing letters in shortened words

points.label: Examples
points.text: don't (do not), can't (cannot), it's (it is), won't (will not)

slides.inSimpleWords: Apostrophes show missing letters in short words!

slides.title: Quotation Marks Show Dialogue
slides.storyContext: When someone speaks, their exact words go inside quotation marks.

points.label: Dialogue format
points.text: Arun said, 'I like mangoes.'

points.label: The marks
points.text: Quotation marks show exactly what was said

slides.inSimpleWords: Quotation marks show what someone said!

slides.title: Fix the Contractions
slides.storyContext: Arun writes contractions but misses some apostrophes. Can you fix them?

example.solution: don't, can't, won't, isn't (Apostrophes show missing letters)

slides.inSimpleWords: Add apostrophes to show missing letters!

slides.title: Punctuation Mix-Up
slides.storyContext: Maya's sentence is missing punctuation. Can you fix it?

points.label: Broken sentence
points.text: I like apples oranges and grapes

points.label: Fix it
points.text: Add commas and a period

slides.inSimpleWords: Add commas between items and a period at the end!

slides.title: The Grammar of Punctuation
slides.storyContext: A complete guide to when and why we use each punctuation mark.

points.label: Ending marks
points.text: Period (.), question mark (?), exclamation mark (!)

points.label: Separators
points.text: Comma (,) divides items in a list

points.label: Special uses
points.text: Apostrophe (') for contractions, quotation marks ('')  for dialogue

slides.inSimpleWords: Different marks have different important jobs!

slides.title: Arun's Exciting Discovery
slides.storyContext: Arun realizes punctuation marks are like traffic signs for sentences!

points.label: Traffic analogy
points.text: Period = Stop. Question mark = What? Exclamation = Wow!

slides.inSimpleWords: Punctuation marks guide readers through your writing!

slides.title: Create a Punctuated Paragraph
slides.storyContext: Write 3-4 sentences about your favorite activity, using all types of punctuation!

points.label: Must use
points.text: At least one period, one question mark, and one comma

slides.inSimpleWords: Write sentences with different punctuation marks!

slides.title: Punctuation Powers
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya celebrate mastering all punctuation marks!

points.label: End your sentences
points.text: With . ? or ! to show what kind of sentence it is

points.label: Separate items
points.text: Use commas in lists

points.label: Special marks
points.text: Apostrophes for contractions, quotes for dialogue

slides.inSimpleWords: Every punctuation mark makes your writing clearer!

subject: English
title: Arun and Maya's One and Many Adventure
hook: Discover how English words change when there's one thing or many things!

slides.title: Singular = One Thing
slides.storyContext: Arun holds up one apple. He says 'apple' — that's singular!

points.label: Singular
points.text: Singular means ONE thing or person

slides.inSimpleWords: Singular is the word for ONE thing!

image.alt: Singular = One Thing — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Plural = Many Things
slides.storyContext: Maya holds up five apples. She says 'apples' — that's plural!

points.label: Plural
points.text: Plural means MORE than ONE (many things)

slides.inSimpleWords: Plural is the word for MANY things!

image.alt: Plural = Many Things — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Most Plurals Add 's'
slides.storyContext: Arun shows: one cat is 'cat', many cats are 'cats'. Just add 's'!

points.label: Add s
points.text: cat → cats, book → books, dog → dogs

slides.inSimpleWords: Add 's' to most words to make them plural!

image.alt: Most Plurals Add 's' — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Words Ending in 'x, z, s' Add 'es'
slides.storyContext: Maya shows: box → boxes, buzz → buzzes, class → classes!

points.label: Add es
points.text: Words ending in x, z, s, sh, ch add 'es'

slides.inSimpleWords: Add 'es' to words ending in x, z, s, sh, ch!

image.alt: Words Ending in 'x, z, s' Add 'es' — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Words Ending in 'y' Change
slides.storyContext: Arun says: one baby, many babies. The 'y' becomes 'ies'!

points.label: y to ies
points.text: baby → babies, lady → ladies, city → cities

slides.inSimpleWords: Change 'y' to 'ies' for words ending in consonant+y!

image.alt: Words Ending in 'y' Change — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Irregular Plurals
slides.storyContext: Maya shows words that don't follow the rules!

example.problem: Singular: child, foot, tooth, person. Plural?
example.solution: children, feet, teeth, people. These are IRREGULAR!

slides.inSimpleWords: Some words change completely to make plural!

image.alt: Irregular Plurals — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Practice with Sentences
slides.storyContext: Arun says 'I have one book.' Maya says 'I have many books.'

points.label: Singular sentence
points.text: The boy plays.

points.label: Plural sentence
points.text: The boys play.

slides.inSimpleWords: Use singular and plural words in your sentences!

image.alt: Practice with Sentences — Singular and Plural

slides.title: Singular and Plural
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya make a list of singular and plural word pairs!

points.label: Add s
points.text: cat → cats, book → books

points.label: Add es
points.text: box → boxes, class → classes

points.label: Irregular
points.text: child → children, foot → feet

slides.inSimpleWords: One thing = singular. Many = plural. Learn the rules!

image.alt: Singular and Plural — Singular and Plural

slides.title: What is Singular and Plural?
slides.storyContext: Understanding the difference between one and many.

points.label: Singular form
points.text: Used when there is exactly ONE of something

points.label: Plural form
points.text: Used when there are TWO or MORE of something

slides.inSimpleWords: Singular = 1. Plural = 2 or more!

slides.title: The Simple 's' Rule
slides.storyContext: Most words just need an 's' to become plural.

points.label: Regular plurals
points.text: pen → pens, desk → desks, flower → flowers, friend → friends

points.label: Quick tip
points.text: Most English words just add 's' to show more than one

slides.inSimpleWords: For most words, just add 's' to make them plural!

slides.title: Making Simple Plurals
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya practice adding 's' to everyday words.

example.solution: Plural: apples, shoes, tables, pencils (just add 's')

slides.inSimpleWords: Add 's' to change singular words to plural!

slides.title: The 'es' Rule
slides.storyContext: Some words need 'es' instead of just 's'.

points.label: Words ending in s, x, z, sh, ch
points.text: bus → buses, box → boxes, buzz → buzzes, brush → brushes, church → churches

slides.inSimpleWords: Words ending in s, x, z, sh, ch need 'es'!

slides.title: Adding 'es' to Words
slides.storyContext: Maya shows words that need 'es' for the plural.
slides.inSimpleWords: Add 'es' to words ending in s, x, z, sh, ch!

slides.title: The 'y' to 'ies' Rule
slides.storyContext: Words ending in consonant+y have a special change.

points.label: y to ies rule
points.text: When 'y' comes after a consonant, change 'y' to 'ies'

points.label: Examples
points.text: candy → candies, family → families, story → stories

slides.inSimpleWords: Change 'y' to 'ies' when 'y' follows a consonant!

slides.title: Changing 'y' to 'ies'
slides.storyContext: Arun practices the tricky 'y' to 'ies' rule.

example.solution: Plural: happies→no wait! happies isn't right. Let me try: happy→happ ies (happy → happies, angry → angries — wait, happy → happier, singular happy → plural: people who are happy. Actually: bunny → bunnies, puppy → puppies)

slides.inSimpleWords: Change y to ies: bunny → bunnies, puppy → puppies!

slides.title: Irregular Plural Changes
slides.storyContext: Some words don't follow any rule—they're irregular!

points.label: Common irregulars
points.text: child → children, man → men, woman → women, foot → feet, tooth → teeth

points.label: Must memorize
points.text: These change completely, not just by adding letters

slides.inSimpleWords: Some words change completely—they're irregular!

slides.title: Spot the Correct Plural
slides.storyContext: Can you choose the right plural form?

points.label: Question 1
points.text: One is 'book', many are: bookes or books?

points.label: Question 2
points.text: One is 'box', many are: boxs or boxes?

points.label: Question 3
points.text: One is 'child', many are: childs or children?

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose the correct plural form!

slides.title: Singular and Plural in Sentences
slides.storyContext: The verb also changes depending on singular or plural!

points.label: Singular sentence
points.text: The dog runs. The cat sleeps.

points.label: Plural sentence
points.text: The dogs run. The cats sleep.

slides.inSimpleWords: When you use plural, the verb changes too!

slides.title: Matching Verbs with Singular and Plural
slides.storyContext: The verb 'is' and 'are' change based on singular/plural.

example.problem: One cat are happy. Two cats is happy.
example.solution: One cat IS happy. Two cats ARE happy. (is for singular, are for plural)

slides.inSimpleWords: Use 'is' with singular, 'are' with plural!

slides.title: Fill in Singular or Plural
slides.storyContext: Choose the correct word—singular or plural—to complete the sentence.

points.label: Sentence 1
points.text: I have one ___ (pencil/pencils)

points.label: Sentence 2
points.text: They have many ___ (friend/friends)

points.label: Sentence 3
points.text: She sees one ___ (butterfly/butterflies)

slides.inSimpleWords: Choose singular or plural for each sentence!

slides.title: Unchanging Plurals
slides.storyContext: Some words stay the same in singular and plural!

points.label: Same word both ways
points.text: sheep, fish, deer, moose (one sheep, many sheep)

slides.inSimpleWords: Some words don't change at all—sheep is sheep!

slides.title: Arun's Word Collection Game
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya collect singular and plural pairs from their textbook!

points.label: The game
points.text: Find pairs that show singular → plural transformations

slides.inSimpleWords: Collect pairs of singular and plural words!

slides.title: All the Plural Rules
slides.storyContext: Arun and Maya create the ultimate Singular and Plural guide!

points.label: Most words
points.text: Add 's': cat → cats, book → books

points.label: Words ending in s, x, z, sh, ch
points.text: Add 'es': box → boxes, dish → dishes

points.label: Words ending in consonant+y
points.text: Change to 'ies': baby → babies

points.label: Irregular words
points.text: Change completely: child → children

slides.inSimpleWords: Learn all the rules to make singular into plural!

slides.title: Write a Paragraph with Singular and Plural
slides.storyContext: Write 4 sentences using both singular and plural words!

points.label: Rules to follow
points.text: Use at least 3 singular words and 3 plural words

slides.inSimpleWords: Write sentences using singular AND plural words!
